title: The simple past: el indefinido
topic: pretérito indefinido of regular verbs; ayer, el año pasado, en 2019
why: After the perfecto, here's the other big past tense, the indefinido, the one used for yesterday, last week or last year. The lesson nails down the regular endings, the written accent (hablo / habló), the spellings llegué, busqué, empecé, and above all the choice between perfecto and indefinido depending on the time marker, before the irregular verbs of the next lesson.

The endings of the indefinido

The pretérito indefinido is the equivalent of the English simple past (“she spoke”, “we ate”): a completed action, used all the time in everyday speech. For regular verbs, there's one set of endings for -ar and a single shared set for -er and -ir.

hablarcomervivir
yohablécomíviví
túhablastecomisteviviste
él, ella, ustedhablócomióvivió
nosotros, nosotrashablamoscomimosvivimos
vosotros, vosotrashablasteiscomisteisvivisteis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablaroncomieronvivieron

The written accent changes everything

The yo and él forms have a written accent on the last syllable. Without it, the word becomes a different tense:

PresentIndefinido
hablo: I speakhabló: he spoke
trabajo: I worktrabajó: she worked
llego: I arrivellegó: he arrived

For nosotros, -ar and -ir verbs have the same form in the present and in the indefinido: hablamos, vivimos. The time marker makes the difference: Ayer hablamos con Carmen (yesterday we spoke with Carmen).

Another very common trap, even among Spaniards: the tú form never takes a final -s. You write hablaste, comiste, not “hablastes”.

", "

A finished time

The indefinido tells of an action completed in a period that's also over, cut off from the present: yesterday, last week, last year, in 2019. It's the partner of the perfecto from the previous lesson: the time marker decides, much like the English choice between “I worked” and “I've worked”.

Time markerExampleTranslation
ayerAyer cené con Lucía.Yesterday I had dinner with Lucía.
anocheAnoche volvimos tarde.Last night we came back late.
anteayerAnteayer llovió mucho.The day before yesterday it rained a lot.
el lunes pasadoEl lunes pasado empecé un curso.Last Monday I started a course.
la semana pasadaLa semana pasada trabajé mucho.Last week I worked a lot.
el año pasadoEl año pasado viajaron a Italia.Last year they traveled to Italy.
en 2019, en agostoEn 2019 viví en Londres.In 2019 I lived in London.
hace dos añosHace dos años conocí a Marta.Two years ago I met Marta.

Perfecto or indefinido?

Ask yourself just one question: is the period over? If it's still going on (hoy, esta semana, este año), it's the perfecto. If it's over (ayer, la semana pasada, el año pasado), it's the indefinido.

Period not over: perfectoPeriod over: indefinido
Hoy he comido paella.Ayer comí paella.
Esta semana he trabajado mucho.La semana pasada trabajé mucho.
Este año he viajado a Roma.El año pasado viajé a Roma.

Hace + length of time = “ago”, but it comes first: hace dos años (two years ago), hace una semana (a week ago). Don't confuse it with hay, which means “there is, there are”.

In Latin America, people use the indefinido almost everywhere, even with “today”, just like American English: Hoy comí paella. In Madrid, people say Hoy he comido paella.

", "

Spelling: llegué, busqué, empecé

In the yo form, the ending -é forces some verbs to change a letter to keep the same sound. It's only a matter of spelling: the pronunciation doesn't change.

Verbs ending in…ChangeExamples (yo)But (él)
-garg → gullegué, pagué, juguéllegó, pagó, jugó
-carc → qubusqué, saqué, toquébuscó, sacó, tocó
-zarz → cempecé, crucé, comencéempezó, cruzó, comenzó

Without the u, “llegé” would be pronounced with a jota (the throaty h sound); without the qu, “buscé” would be read with the sound of z. And in Spanish you almost never write ze or zi: you write ce, ci.

Ayer llegué tarde, busqué un taxi y pagué veinte euros.Yesterday I arrived late, looked for a taxi and paid twenty euros.

No more stem changes!

Good news: the -ar and -er verbs that change their stem in the present are completely regular in the indefinido. The “boot” disappears:

PresentIndefinido
vuelvo (volver)volví, volvió
pienso (pensar)pensé, pensó
encuentro (encontrar)encontré, encontró
empiezo (empezar)empecé, empezó
juego (jugar)jugué, jugó

-ir verbs like pedir or dormir change a little in the third person: you'll see them in the next lesson, along with the big irregular verbs (ser, ir, tener, hacer…).
